**The Slowest Goodbye**

There's a fact I return to more often than I probably should: the Moon is leaving. Not dramatically, not on any timescale that could frighten anyone. It drifts away at roughly the rate your fingernails grow, about four centimeters a year. We know this with eerie precision. Half a century ago astronauts left mirrors on its surface, and we've been bouncing lasers off them ever since, timing the round trip of light down to the millimeter.

It leaves because we push it. Earth spins once a day while the Moon takes a month to lap the planet, so the ocean's tidal bulge—dragged around by friction—is carried slightly *ahead* of the Moon's position. That forward-leaning hump of water has gravity, and it tugs the Moon forward like a hand cupped behind a rolling marble. The Moon gains energy and climbs to a higher orbit. Earth pays the bill with its own spin: thanks to conservation of angular momentum, our days are stretching by a few thousandths of a second per century. Ancient corals grew in bands like tree rings, and when you cut into specimens 380 million years old, you find about 400 daily bands per year. Days used to be shorter. The planet has been slowly winding down, and the Moon has been cashing in the difference, centimeter by centimeter.

For now, though, something extraordinary holds. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon—and, by pure accident, about 400 times farther away. Their apparent sizes match. Nothing requires this to be true, and it will not remain true. As the Moon recedes, its disk shrinks against ours. Some eclipses already come up short, the Moon failing to cover the Sun and leaving a blazing ring instead of night. Every century, totality slides further toward extinction. Give it six hundred million years, give or take, and the last one occurs—the final time daylight dies at noon—after which Earth will know only rings of fire.

Which quietly reframes what a total eclipse is. Not merely beautiful: *timely.* When it comes—air temperature dropping, birds homing mid-afternoon, a 360-degree false dawn burning along the whole horizon while the sky goes a color it has no business going at noon, and then the corona blooming like a cold white flower—you are watching something permitted only inside a narrow corridor of cosmic history. A dinosaur would have seen the Moon swallow the Sun with room to spare. A creature of the far future will see it fall short. We inherited the sweet spot, in a lottery we didn't enter.

I suspect nearly everything lovely works this way: windows rather than monuments. And any observer is bound to wake up inside some such window, because observers arise wherever the coincidences happen to be passing through. Eclipses are just unusually punctual about telling us so.

So if you ever get the chance, go stand in the path of totality. Understand that you're attending a limited engagement. The two oldest clocks in the sky agree perfectly for a minute or two—the one thing in nature that closes on schedule because of a fingernail's-width drift, four centimeters a year, the slowest goodbye ever conducted. Then the light comes back like a held breath released, and the separation resumes, patient and polite, on its way to a future where nobody will see this at all.
